warnings: Escitalopram in hepatic impairment: start at 5 mg and do not exceed 10 mg daily.
SSRIs increase the bleeding risk with thrombocytopenia and portal hypertension, and can cause hyponatremia.
Pantoprazole: long-term proton pump inhibitor use is associated with hepatic encephalopathy and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in cirrhosis; review the indication.
IV potassium chloride: no faster than 10 mEq/h through a peripheral line; faster rates only through a central line with continuous ECG monitoring.
Avoid benzodiazepines, opioids and sedating antihistamines in hepatic encephalopathy.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Potassium 2.6 mEq/L and magnesium 1.6 mg/dL with creatinine 1.6 and BUN 28 mg/dL (pre-renal AKI) after diarrhea; WBC 7.8 and CRP 4; bilirubin 3.4 mg/dL, albumin 2.5 g/dL and INR 1.7 (Child-Pugh C, MELD-Na 21); ammonia 94 µmol/L supports but does not grade HE.
action_criteria.label: Core laboratory work-up: blood count, electrolytes, renal and liver function, glucose, INR, ammonia and CRP, with toxicology where alcohol or drugs are in question
action_criteria.rationale: Confirms liver dysfunction and identifies metabolic and infective precipitants; magnesium because diarrhea with severe hypokalemia makes magnesium loss likely and it impairs potassium repletion.

action_criteria.rationale: Escitalopram prolongs the QT interval, which hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia aggravate, and metformin is unsafe with acute kidney injury in decompensated cirrhosis.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not give benzodiazepines or other sedatives for agitation or sleep: they precipitate and prolong hepatic encephalopathy; manage agitation with reorientation, a safe environment and treatment of the precipitant (EASL 2022).
Do not prescribe opioids or other sedating drugs: they precipitate and prolong HE; for pain use acetaminophen up to 2 g per day.
Do not increase lactulose or titrate it to the ammonia level: the target is 2-3 soft bowel movements per day, and over-titration caused this episode.
Do not give loperamide or another opioid antidiarrheal: reduce the lactulose instead.
required_recommendations: Reduce lactulose to the dose that gives 2-3 soft bowel movements per day (currently 8-10 loose stools per day with potassium 2.6); correct potassium and volume, and investigate persisting diarrhea rather than attributing it to lactulose.

Replace potassium to 4.0 mEq/L or more with IV potassium chloride under ECG monitoring, because hypokalemia increases renal ammoniagenesis, and replace magnesium (1.6 mg/dL) so that potassium repletion holds.
Treat the pre-renal AKI (creatinine 1.6, BUN 28): replace the diarrheal losses with IV crystalloid, and give albumin 1 g/kg per day for 2 days if creatinine does not improve (EASL 2018).
Hold metformin during the AKI and decompensated cirrhosis (lactic acidosis risk) and manage glucose with insulin.
Hold escitalopram while the QTc is prolonged and potassium and magnesium are low; restart at no more than 10 mg daily (the maximum in hepatic impairment) once a repeat ECG shows a normal QTc.
Continue rifaximin 550 mg twice daily with lactulose as secondary prophylaxis (ACG 2026; EASL 2022).
If overt HE recurs despite lactulose and rifaximin with no other precipitant, discuss TIPS diameter reduction with the interventional radiology team (EASL 2022).
Review the pantoprazole indication and stop it if there is none (long-term proton pump inhibitors are associated with HE and SBP in cirrhosis).
Refer for liver transplant assessment: decompensated cirrhosis with overt HE, MELD-Na 21 (EASL 2018).

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE workup.
Early-onset AD genetic panel has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the diagnosis under consideration.
Visual evoked potentials have no role in HE workup; no demyelinating process is on the differential.

accepted: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade III), post-TIPS alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C, MELD-Na 21), precipitated by lactulose overuse (8-10 stools/day) causing severe hypokalemia (K 2.6), hypovolemia and pre-renal AKI; the patent TIPS is a structural background contributor.

differential.key_features: Doppler shows a patent shunt with in-stent velocities 112-136 cm/s and no stenosis or thrombosis; shunt dysfunction presents with recurrent ascites or bleeding rather than HE.
The patent shunt predisposes to HE, but this episode has a clear precipitant (lactulose overuse with hypokalemia, hypovolemia and AKI).
Escitalopram 10 mg is within the maximum dose in hepatic impairment and does not cause asterixis; its relevance here is the QT risk with hypokalemia.
Reports 4 months of abstinence; serum ethanol below 10 mg/dL and CIWA 3.
No ascites on examination or ultrasound; afebrile, WBC 7.8; no paracentesis indicated.
Creatinine 1.6 with BUN 28 after days of diarrhea and minimal intake is pre-renal; HRS-AKI is considered only if creatinine fails to improve after volume expansion with albumin for 48 hours.

key_clinical_evidence: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grade, evidence of liver disease and exclusion of other causes of altered mental status (ACG 2026; EASL 2022).

An elevated ammonia neither grades nor confirms hepatic encephalopathy and repeat levels are not used to guide treatment; a normal ammonia in a confused patient with cirrhosis should prompt a search for another cause (ACG 2026 recommendation 5 and key concept 14; EASL 2022).
Child-Pugh C (12: bilirubin 3.4 3, albumin 2.5 3, INR 1.7 2, no ascites 1, HE grade III 3); MELD-Na 21 (creatinine 1.6, bilirubin 3.4, INR 1.7, sodium 142, bounded at 137).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection, GI bleeding, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia, hyponatremia), constipation, sedatives, dehydration and renal failure.

Lactulose over-titration causes dehydration, hypokalemia, hypernatremia and pre-renal AKI, all of which worsen HE; the dose is titrated to 2-3 soft bowel movements per day, not to the ammonia level (ACG 2026; EASL 2022).

After TIPS, a patent shunt predisposes to HE, whereas shunt dysfunction presents with recurrent ascites or bleeding; Doppler documents the shunt, and diameter reduction is considered for HE that recurs despite lactulose and rifaximin (EASL 2022).

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Escitalopram 10 mg is within the maximum dose in hepatic impairment and is not the driver of the encephalopathy; its relevance is the QT risk with hypokalemia. Lactulose overuse with hypokalemia is the dominant precipitant.
red_herrings.data_point: Escitalopram increased from 5 to 10 mg one month ago
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute HE to escitalopram toxicity / SSRI accumulation.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A patent TIPS predisposes to HE, but a sudden worsening needs a precipitant search: Doppler shows a patent shunt with normal velocities, and lactulose overuse with hypokalemia and AKI is the proximate cause. Shunt reduction is considered only if HE recurs despite lactulose and rifaximin.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Assume TIPS is the cause and request shunt reduction; ignore lactulose dosing.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. H. is a 55-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis who underwent TIPS (transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt) placement 4 months ago for refractory ascites, and has been on rifaximin and lactulose prophylaxis since. His daughter (visiting from out of town) noticed he was confused and disoriented when she arrived, noting he could not remember the day, was repeating himself, and seemed 'out of it.' She was unable to reach him by phone for 3 days before arriving at his apartment. He appeared to have been eating and drinking minimally. His apartment had evidence of diarrhea — his toilet had been used repeatedly with watery stool. His daughter estimated he had 8-10 loose stools per day for the past 3-4 days. A lactulose bottle refilled 10 days earlier was nearly empty, about twice the prescribed amount. He denies alcohol use. He had recently increased his escitalopram dose from 5 mg to 10 mg one month ago.

neurological_exam.additional: Known to TIPS clinic — last TIPS check-up was 3 months ago (shunt patent). Doppler ultrasound not yet performed this admission. Jaundice visible. No ascites on exam.
